S:
  2 week Hx exertional central chest tightness
  Described as heavy pressing sensation
  Triggered by exertion (pushing wheelbarrow, climbing stairs)
  Lasts 5-10 mins, resolves with rest
  Radiated to left arm once
  No pain at rest
  Mild SOB with pain, no nausea/vomiting
  Occasional post-prandial burning (rice), but current pain is different
  No tenderness on chest wall palpation
  Smokes 20 cigarettes/day for 30 years
  Alcohol: weekends, 2-3 glasses
  Hx of high BP identified at medical camp last year, not followed up
  Father had MI age ~60
  No regular medications or known allergies
  Patient's ideas: Unclear what he thinks is going on, but worried about the chest pain.
  Patient's concerns: Worried it might be a heart attack.
  Patient's expectations: Reassurance that it isn't a current heart attack.

O:
  Pulse 88 regular
  BP 150/95
  Heart sounds normal, no murmurs
  Lungs clear
  No chest wall tenderness on palpation

A:
  Angina suspected

P:
  ECG today
  Urgent referral to Cardiology clinic for bloods and further tests
  Start Aspirin (dose not specified) after ECG
  Smoking cessation advice given, provide details of clinics
  Discussed BP management, will confirm and likely start medication at next visit
  Safety netting: Advised to go straight to hospital ED if chest pain occurs at rest, lasts >15 mins, or doesn't settle with rest

S:
  6yo F presents with 3 days fever (started Fri eve)
  Fever up to 39°C, partially responsive to paracetamol
  Associated symptoms: headache, retro-orbital eye pain, vomiting x2 this morning, anorexia
  Reduced fluid intake (drinks little when prompted)
  Normal urine output
  No rash, bleeding (gums, nose, urine, stool)
  Minimal cough
  Local dengue cases reported nearby; construction site with water collection
  No previous history of dengue or other significant illness
  No regular medications, no known allergies
  Patient's ideas: Is it dengue?
  Patient's concerns: Frightened due to local dengue cases
  Patient's expectations: Wants to know if it is dengue

O:
  Temp 38.9°C
  Mild conjunctival injection
  Throat slightly red
  Chest clear on auscultation
  Abdomen soft, non-tender, liver not enlarged
  No rash or petechiae
  Capillary refill normal
  Alert and well hydrated appearance

A:
  Possible Dengue Fever (day 3)
  Viral fever (differential diagnosis)

P:
  Full Blood Count (FBC)
  Dengue NS1 antigen test
  Paracetamol only for fever (avoid ibuprofen/NSAIDs)
  Encourage oral fluids frequently (water, king coconut, kanji, jeewani)
  Review tomorrow with blood results
  Safety netting: return immediately or go to hospital if worsening symptoms (severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, lethargy/confusion, oliguria, cold extremities) especially after fever subsides

S:
  Routine diabetes check-up
  Feels generally 'not too bad'
  Reports increased thirst
  Reports burning, tingling in both feet at night for ~2 months, sometimes waking her up
  Feet also feel a little numb
  Denies wounds or ulcers on feet; checks regularly
  Medications: Metformin 1g BD, Gliclazide 80mg AM, Losartan 50mg OD
  Denies episodes of low sugar (shaking, sweating, faintness)
  Checks blood sugar at home; fasting glucose ~160-170 mg/dL
  Last HbA1c 8.4%
  Diet: Rice in afternoon, bread/string hoppers at night. Tea with 2 spoons sugar BD.
  Reports eating a 'good plate' of rice
  Limited exercise due to knee problems
  Denies chest pain or breathlessness
  Eyes feel alright, but eye check > 1 year ago
  Patient's ideas: Unclear what is causing the foot symptoms.
  Patient's concerns: Worried about the burning/tingling in feet.
  Patient's expectations: Asked if neuropathy can be cured.

O:
  BP 140/85 mmHg
  Weight 68 kg
  Feet: Skin healthy, no cracks/ulcers. Pulses palpable bilaterally.
  Neuropathy screen: Reduced sensation to monofilament in toes; ankle sensation intact.

A:
  Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM)
  Poor glycemic control
  Hypertension (HTN)
  Diabetic peripheral neuropathy

P:
  Increase Gliclazide to 80mg BD
  Start Atorvastatin 1mg at night
  Order HbA1c, kidney function tests, cholesterol, urine protein
  Referral to eye screening service
  Dietary advice: Reduce rice intake by half, increase vegetables/dhal. Eliminate sugar from tea.
  Exercise advice: Start with 15 min walking daily on flat surface
  Foot care advice: Daily inspection for wounds/changes
  Review in 3 months with test results

S:
  Asthma symptoms worsening for ~1 month.
  History of childhood asthma, quiescent for years.
  Symptoms: wheezing, nocturnal cough (wakes 2x/week).
  Using blue inhaler frequently: 4-5 times/week, sometimes twice daily.
  Ran out of blue inhaler last week.
  Only uses blue inhaler (salbutamol).
  Triggers: dust (sweeping), dry weather, stress (exams).
  No recent fever or cold symptoms.
  No chest pain.
  Can walk and speak normally currently.
  Admitted to hospital overnight for asthma as a child, mother reports.
  Never in ICU or required repeated nebulisers.
  Non-smoker.
  No one at home smokes.

O:
  RR 18/min.
  SpO2 98% on room air.
  Mild wheeze heard bilaterally on expiration.
  Peak flow: best of three = 380 L/min.
  Inhaler technique: pressing and breathing too fast.

A:
  Uncontrolled asthma.
  Asthma exacerbation triggered by dust/stress.

P:
  Prescribe beclometasone (brown inhaler) 2 puffs AM and PM daily.
  Continue salbutamol (blue inhaler) PRN for symptoms.
  Provide spacer device.
  Educate on correct inhaler technique with spacer.
  Advise rinsing mouth after beclometasone use.
  Environmental control: wet-dusting or mask when sweeping.
  Provide written asthma action plan.
  Safety netting: seek immediate medical attention if severe breathlessness unresponsive to salbutamol.
  Review in 1 month: recheck peak flow, assess symptom control.

note_plain:
S:
  6 week hx burning epigastric pain
  Pain worse when hungry & at night (wakes patient)
  Pain relieved by food/Gelusil
  Pain located top of stomach, below chest, midline
  Pain described as 'fire inside', sometimes gnawing
  No pain radiating to back
  Occasional burning up chest after late meals
  No recent weight loss (possibly gained)
  Normal appetite
  No dysphagia
  No vomiting
  No haematemesis or coffee ground vomitus
  Normal stool colour, no melaena
  Takes ibuprofen 3-4 days/week (sometimes more) for back pain >1 year
  Drinks arrack weekends (~quarter bottle/night)
  Non-smoker
  Irregular meals due to delivery work
  Reports job stress (targets, traffic)
  Patient's ideas: Thinks it's his stomach.
  Patient's concerns: Asks if it is serious.
  Patient's expectations: Wants to know what to do.

O:
  Mild epigastric tenderness on palpation
  Abdomen otherwise soft, no lumps
  No pallor noted in eyes

A:
  Acid damage/irritation/ulcer formation in stomach lining
  Likely exacerbated by ibuprofen use
  Contributing factors: irregular meals, alcohol, stress

P:
  Stop ibuprofen immediately
  Start paracetamol for back pain (discuss further later)
  Prescribe omeprazole 1 tab daily before breakfast x 4 weeks
  Order stool test for H. pylori
  If H. pylori positive, add antibiotics (details not specified)
  Advise regular meals (every 3-4 hours)
  Advise reducing alcohol intake
  Review in 2 weeks with stool result
  Safety netting: Attend hospital immediately if vomiting blood or melaena occurs
  Consider endoscopy if symptoms persist after 4 weeks or warning signs develop

S:
  Patient reports a 'funny turn' yesterday evening around 6pm
  Sudden onset right hand weakness; difficulty gripping teacup
  Slurred speech reported by daughter
  Symptoms lasted ~15 minutes, resolved completely
  No loss of consciousness, falls, fits or jerking movements
  No headache or visual changes reported
  First episode of this type
  Currently asymptomatic; denies weakness, facial droop, speech difficulty
  History of hypertension, takes amlodipine intermittently
  Borderline diabetes reported
  Stopped cholesterol medication long ago
  Smokes 5-6 cigarettes/day for 50 years
  Reports occasional palpitations ('heart does a little dance')
  Patient's ideas: Thinks it was 'probably nothing', a 'funny turn'
  Patient's concerns: Worried about the seriousness of the irregular heartbeat
  Patient's expectations: Wanted reassurance that everything is normal and to go home

O:
  BP 165/95 mmHg
  Pulse irregularly irregular
  Neurological exam: Strength equal in both hands, symmetrical smile, no drift with arms raised, speech clear ('British constitution')
  Cardiac auscultation: Irregular rhythm, no murmurs
  Lungs clear

A:
  Transient ischaemic attack (TIA) / mini-stroke
  Atrial fibrillation suspected
  Hypertension, poorly controlled
  Smoking
  Borderline diabetes

P:
  ECG performed in clinic
  Aspirin 300mg given immediately
  Urgent referral to medical assessment unit at base hospital today
  Safety netting: Advised to attend ED immediately if symptoms recur

S:
  6 week history of burning epigastric pain, worse when hungry & at night, relieved by food/Gelusil.
  New onset black tarry stools (melena) x 3 in last ~36 hrs, foul smelling.
  Postural dizziness ('head spins') on standing quickly, near syncope this morning.
  Unexplained sweating & weakness.
  Mild dyspnoea on exertion (climbing stairs).
  Regular ibuprofen use for back pain, ~3-4 days/week for >1 year.
  Weekend alcohol use: Arrack, quarter bottle or more.
  No known history of ulcer.
  No blood thinners/aspirin.
  Patient's ideas: Believes it is 'gastritis', which he has had for weeks.
  Patient's concerns: Expresses fear following the doctor's explanation.
  Patient's expectations: Initially hoped to drive himself to hospital.

O:
  Pale conjunctivae.
  BP 100/70 mmHg.
  Pulse 104 bpm.
  Epigastric tenderness on palpation.

A:
  Likely bleeding peptic ulcer.
  Significant blood loss leading to hypovolemia/anaemia.

P:
  Urgent hospital admission via ambulance.
  Referral letter written.
  Inform patient's wife.
  Stop ibuprofen immediately.
  Safety netting: Advise patient to inform ambulance crew if vomiting blood or feeling faint.

S:
  Acute SOB since yesterday morning
  Difficulty breathing even walking short distances
  Sudden onset while hanging washing
  Sharp right-sided chest pain, like a knife
  Pain worse on deep inspiration
  Taking small breaths due to pain
  No significant cough
  No fever, chills or phlegm
  No haemoptysis
  Right calf swelling for 3 days
  Calf pain on walking, feels warm
  Swelling started after long overnight bus journey to Jaffna last week
  Leg symptoms preceded breathing problems
  Takes combined oral contraceptive pill daily for 5 years
  No personal history of blood clots (DVT/PE)
  No family history of blood clots
  Non-smoker
  Patient's ideas: Thought leg swelling might be muscle strain from bus journey
  Patient's concerns: Worried about the danger/severity of a clot in the lung
  Patient's expectations: Needs to go to hospital today

O:
  RR 24/min (tachypnoeic)
  SpO2 92% on room air
  Pulse 110 bpm, regular (tachycardic)
  BP 125/80 mmHg
  Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally
  Right calf swollen, approx. 3cm larger circumference than left
  Right calf warm and tender on palpation
  Left calf normal

A:
  Suspected deep vein thrombosis (DVT) right leg
  Suspected pulmonary embolism (PE)

P:
  Urgent hospital admission via ambulance
  Commence oxygen therapy
  Referral to hospital for CTPA (implied)
  Initiate anticoagulation (blood thinning injections) in hospital
  Advise stopping combined oral contraceptive pill
  Discuss alternative contraception post-treatment

note_plain:
S:
  6yo F presents with 4 days fever [1].
  Today acutely drowsy, difficult to wake [1].
  Reduced intake: nothing drunk today (water, king coconut) [5].
  Vomited 4x since last night [5].
  Last urine output ~5am this morning; usually frequent urination [7].
  No bleeding (gums, nose, vomit) [8].
  No rash observed by mother [8].
  Mottled skin on legs noted by mother [9].
  Cold hands/feet, hot body noted ~1hr ago [9, 11].
  No fits or shaking observed [13].
  Dengue contact in lane (neighbour recovered from hospital) [14].
  Two more houses in lane now have fever [15].
  Patient's ideas: Suspects dengue [17].
  Patient's concerns: Worried about Sanuki's prognosis ('Is she going to be alright?') [19].
  Patient's expectations: Reassurance about outcome [19].

O:
  Rousable but very drowsy [16].
  Temp 39.5°C [16].
  Hands cold to wrists, body hot [16].
  Capillary refill time 4 seconds [16].
  Pulse 145/min, weak [16].
  Legs mottled [16].
  Abdomen: winces slightly on palpation [16].
  Neck: no stiffness [16].
  Skin: no rash, no petechiae/purpura noted [16].

A:
  Shock (likely secondary to severe dengue or serious bacterial infection) [18].

P:
  Call ambulance for immediate transfer to General Hospital [20].
  Referral note to hospital detailing fever, shock signs, suspected severe dengue [22].
  Advise NPO (nothing by mouth) [21].
  Positioning: keep flat with legs slightly elevated [22].
  Safety netting: advise mother to call father from ambulance, stay with child until ambulance arrives [23, 24].

S:
  15yo M presents with acute onset R lower abdominal pain radiating to R groin/testicle, started 5am this morning.
  Pain woke him from sleep, severe ('like a cricket ball hit me'), initially in waves now constant.
  Associated nausea and vomiting x2 (home & en route).
  No fever or chills reported.
  Normal bowel movements yesterday, no diarrhoea/constipation.
  Normal urination, no dysuria or haematuria.
  No recent injury, played cricket yesterday evening without incident.
  No unusual food intake, no other household members unwell.
  Patient initially hesitant to report testicular pain but confirmed R-sided groin/testicular pain is present and severe, worse than abdominal pain.
  Patient's ideas: Unclear what it is, but worried about the pain.
  Patient's concerns: Worried something is wrong with his testicle.
  Patient's expectations: Wants to know if it can be fixed ('Can they untwist it?').

O:
  BP not recorded.
  Abdomen soft on palpation, mild tenderness R lower quadrant deep palpation. No rebound/guarding mentioned.
  Right testicle swollen, high-riding compared to left.
  Right testicle markedly tender on light palpation.
  Absent cremasteric reflex on R side. Normal on L side.

A:
  Clinical diagnosis: Right testicular torsion.

P:
  Immediate referral to surgical team at hospital.
  Phoned surgical registrar with details (15yo M, R testicular pain since 5am, high-riding tender testis, absent cremasteric reflex).
  Patient to go straight to hospital via uncle's motorbike.
  Nil by mouth (NBM) from now.
  Provided referral letter.
  Patient education: Explained diagnosis of torsion, urgency of surgery, importance of reporting testicular pain promptly in future.
